title: The $58 Million Retirement Policy — Pacific Life PDX / Mamboleo Settlement
description: A $58.3 million class-action settlement against Pacific Life Insurance Co. shows how a real policyholder's projected retirement value dropped from $418,141 to $364,351 after a single undisclosed "Performance Factor" was applied — while her actual account value fell to $2,848 after $17,000 in premiums.
sourceCitation: Mamboleo v. Pacific Life Insurance Co., No. 30-2021-01208045-CU-BT-CXC, Orange County Superior Court. Figures sourced directly from the Class Action Complaint (filed 6/29/2021) and the Class Action Settlement Agreement, both public court records. This video uses AI-generated narration. Educational content only, not financial or legal advice.

scenes.narrationText: She paid seventeen thousand dollars into a retirement policy. Two years later, she had two thousand, eight hundred and forty-eight dollars left. This is her actual policy file.
Case file zero-zero-two. Pacific Life Insurance. A fifty-eight-point-three million dollar settlement. Court-approved. Being paid out right now.

When she signed up for a Pacific Life "PDX" policy in 2019, this is the illustration she was shown. By year twenty, at an assumed rate of seven-point-one percent, her policy was projected to be worth four hundred eighteen thousand, one hundred forty-one dollars. Insurance illustrations aren't guarantees. But they're supposed to be a reasonable picture of what you're buying.

Two years later, she asked Pacific Life for an updated illustration on the exact same policy. The assumed rate had barely moved — down to six-point-six-six percent. Just a six percent change. But the projected payout didn't drop six percent. It dropped thirteen percent — more than double what the rate change alone would explain.

Here's her actual account history. Year one: she paid nine thousand, two hundred dollars in premiums. Pacific Life deducted seven thousand, six hundred fifty-three dollars in policy charges. She was left with one thousand, five hundred fifty dollars.
Year two: she paid another seven thousand, eight hundred dollars. Pacific Life deducted six thousand, six hundred eight dollars. Her account value: two thousand, eight hundred forty-eight dollars.
Seventeen thousand dollars paid in. Twenty-eight hundred dollars left. That's not a bad year in the market. That's the policy working exactly as designed.

According to the lawsuit, the reason for the gap was something called the "Performance Factor" — an internal multiplier Pacific Life applied to the illustrated interest rate, starting in year three of the policy.

Pacific Life's own press release bragged about it. The first two Performance Factors it ever calculated were two-point-four-six and four-point-one-eight. At the company's advertised ten percent cap rate, that meant illustrations could show effective returns as high as twenty-four point six percent — or even forty-one point eight percent. The only number Pacific Life actually guaranteed? One-point-zero. No multiplier at all.

And the whole projection depended on Pacific Life earning a fifty percent profit on its own options trades — every single year, for thirty to fifty years. Four of its competitors — MetLife, New York Life, Northwestern Mutual, and OneAmerica — told regulators in writing that assumption was unreasonable. Within three years, Pacific Life cut its cap rate twice. Illustrated performance across the board dropped more than thirty-five percent.

Pacific Life still denies doing anything wrong. But a court disagreed enough to approve fifty-eight-point-three million dollars. Thirty-three million goes directly into the accounts of policyholders whose PDX policies are still active.
Up to twenty-five million goes to free term life insurance for anyone whose policy already lapsed or was surrendered.
If you've ever wondered whether an insurance company is even allowed to do this — a judge just answered that question.
The court gave final approval in May. The money is scheduled to be distributed by September eleventh — this month.
Pacific Life still denies doing anything wrong. A court disagreed enough to approve fifty-eight million dollars.

If you own a Pacific Life PDX policy bought in California between 2016 and 2019 — not PDX 2 — check your mail or email for a settlement notice. Contact Kroll Settlement Administration if you're not sure. If you own any indexed universal life policy — any company — ask directly, in writing: what is my policy's performance factor, multiplier, or bonus rate, and what is the guaranteed minimum? If they can't answer clearly, that's information you're entitled to. This isn't a reason to panic about every policy. It's a reason to read the actual illustration — not just the pitch.
